div.head: PAST BEEF SHOWS.
div.p: PAST BEEF SHOWS.
Sights Which Upset Vege-
tarians.
REMINISCENCES OF, WARRINGTON.

To last week's issue of "The Advertiser's Weekly" Mr. Wallace Gandy, a former War- rington school teacher, contributes an entertain- ing article full of reminiscences of the old town at Christmastide. What a difference this year from Christmases that have been, he states. Years ago in a Northern town I still know very well, the greatest sight of the year was the Beef Show. Beef, game, poultry, pork, cheese ! What a prolific person Dame Nature was, under the guidance of good Cheshire husbandry, to be sure ! The street still called Butteriaarket, and in which recently_ I saw an old wooden beam—a three hundred year old beam of good oak—mark- ing the limit beyond which potatoes niiciht not be sold, had two or three shops, gaily decorated and hung half-way,to the upper storey windows with the dressed carcases of the lesser beasts, and in the centre of the window slab a sight net for a vegetarian to look at! An orange in the jaws of a pig, and holly, 'well berried, curling round its neck.

The street leading to the bridge was even more of a shock to the cult. Twenty years passed over those butchers' heads and they never seemed any older to me. And they were butchers in those days—not merely "purveyors of meat." They slapped the rounds with the flat sides of the hatchets, and could not cry "Buy) buy," for laughing. There never was a joke to laugh at, am sure, but it ,was the infectious spirit that served the then " purveyor" for publicity. Chestnuts and similar nutriment, to be sure— but as an accessory to the much larger fact— the ponderous fact that weighed I-don't-know- how-many pounds, and was fed by one of the "lords of the manor." _
Another " market -" street—horses this time— was full of toy shops and poulterers and pork butchers; more garlands and misplaced oranges, and no golliwogs in those days.
And Other Wonders.

There were many things to wonder at. One was where all this meat was destined, and whether when cooked those barons and turkeys would taste as good as those which I, with‘thirty kindred souls—or stomachs, for I'd no soul, I declare—would valiantly attempt to demolish on Christmas Day. The other wonder was what pigs and oranges had to do with each other. No one knew, but the ritual was observed. What, too, must be said of the stacks of raisins, and all the ingredients of the pudding which all the world but a Briton laughs at. That much,maligned pudding has been. called every bad name by our intellectuals. They even forgot its harmless composition. And one year a very wise doctor, nearly as wise as my grand- mother, and yours, too, dear reader, said the plum pudding was as good as medicine. And so our intellectuals were calmed and conquered. And the Frost.

Does anybody remember, in these days, when the Manchester Ship Canal was merely a great trench, muddy withal, from Eastham Lock to Salford? There was many a good skating year in those days, and I learned the gliding art. Quite sad I felt when, this week, I saw stacks of skates "selling off" at a great London store— as if they were the derelicts of past joyous times.

And frost reminds me of the marvellous win- dow-dressing, as it seemed in those days. Cards in profusion, mottoes, impossible Father Christ- mases, which spoke to us of wolf-threatened rides in sleighs on the Russian plains; boot tops ridiculously carried holly leaves, and mistletoe peeped out of ladies' handbags. Jokes went round, of the man who wanted a comforter and the woman who secured a muff.

div.head: Toast.
div.p: A Toast.

The boys of those days have nearly all gone on stern business. It is difficult to trace where they all are and how they reached their present state of felicity or its opposite. I doubt the large scale of the Beef Show this year. The beef has gone elsewhere—to the men of brawn— and we do not regret it.

div.head: CHRISTMAS CONCERT.
div.p: CHRISTMAS CONCERT.
Children Of Our Lady's Splendid Entertainment.

At Our Lady's School, Latchford, a Christmas concert was given by the children on Saturday. The programme was a long one, and the splen- did manner in which the scholafs performed was greatly due to the efforts of Miss Rourke and the staff.

Dancing was pre-eminent during the 4'fter- noon. the Italian flower girl, who delithted the audience with a national dance, and "La Petite Tonkinoise," which was given by the fantastic mothers, were both well done. A coquette dance, an Irish song and dance, were also presented. A naval troupe sang " Home- ward " and "Where go the ships," and gave dances. The midget dramatists gave "Santa Claus and the mouse " ; the happy mothers, " Husheen "; and the midget volunteers, "Mili- tary movements of the citizen corps." Two songs, "I dunno' where," by the juvenile masked players, and " Rotkin' in de win'," by the coons, were exquisitely rendered. elec- tions from Shakespeare's plays were delightfully played. They were, "Before Agincourt," "The Vanity of Greatness," and the banquet scene from Macbeth." The prologue to Milton's. "-L'Allegro" was well given. "The three ships," "The sea is England's glory," and "Clang, clang," were choruses given by the choir.
_ The 'hanks of an appreciative audience to the staff and children were voiced by the Rev. Father Talton at the close.

div.head: URGENTLY NEEDED!
div.p: URGENTLY NEEDED!
Woollen Comforts For Our Soldiers In The Trenches.

Among the many opportunities of " war work," the voluntary organisation of workers is playing an important part by providing soldiers' comforts for the cold weather. During the past month several large bales of woollen comforts have been dispatched to our brave troops on the Continent, a specially large -con- signment. consisting of mittens, mufflers, socks, belts and helmets, being forwarded last week, in response to an urgent appeal from Sir Edward Ward, the Director-Cheneral of Volun- tary Organisations. This contribution has been acknowledged in the following terms : "I thank you for your generous response to the appeal, and express a hope that the num- ber of comforts available will be even larger during the next few weeks." It will be seen from the above that there is still a large demand for woollen comforts, and we are sure we shall not appeal in vain to the women of Warrington. Contributions towards the next requisition will be gladly received by the various branches of the organisation, which are so enthusiastically carrying on this work, viz., the Women's Liberal Association, the Territorial Association, the Cairo-street, Wes- leyan and Central Working Parties. The depot for the above is Holly House, Sankey-street.

div.head: Palace anti Hippodrome.
div.p: Palace anti Hippodrome.

As this is the season for making gifts, visitors to the Hippbdrorae were especially in- terested in C. H. Charlton's marvellous per- formance. He is, indeed, a famous wizard, and his wonderful kettle is perhaps one of the most astonishing feats of modern conjuring. The audience are invited to call for drinks and favourite beverages are immediately forthcoming and sent down from the stage for consumption. Whiskies of different brands, mild and bitter beer, port, sherry, gin and water, soda and a glass of milk are produced, and then the wonderful kettle is itself sent round for inspection.

Our otit friends, the Marionettes, hajte ad- vanced with the times, and Page's Animated Dolls are to be seen in a topical patriotic and comedy revue. The puppets are worked in the most natural manner possible. There is a vigorous orchestra and the entertainment is complete in every respect. There is a big fight between an aeroplane and a Zepp, the latter being defeated ignominiously.
A splendid show is given by the Four Sisters Martelloni, who are rightly described as Italy's smartest lady acrobats and equilibrists.
Occupying a prominent place on the pro- gramme is Miss Edna ,Lyall, and her render- ing of sonic popular songs is keenly appre- ciated.

Charles Mildare, whistler and vocalist, is always a welcome turn and his popularity .is as strong asoever. Bob Lloyd and June Mon- trose, comedy entertainers, are most diverting, and Kristo and Renee present a novel comedy act which creates much enjoyment.

The management of the Palace and Hippo- drome announce some special, holiday attrac- tions. Topping the bill are Noland and Kiddie, with a refined, dancing act. Next comes Frank Foster, the celebrated tenor, who has. appeared in opera at Covent Garden; Will Hay, the schoolmaster comedian (a rare funny fellow, this—l - saw him a short while ago at the Liverpool Empire)‘; Kelly, West and Reed—a piano, a I fool, a soubrette and an acrobat; Larkum Bros., novelty comedians, in "The New Porter"; and others. div.head: "Cinderella" at Manchester.
div.p: "Cinderella" at Manchester.

Warrington pepple who are visiting Man- chester during the next few weeks should not fail to see that gorgeous pantomime, "Cinderella," at-the Palace Theatre. There need be no fear of arriving home late, for those who do not care to wait for the evening performance have the opportunity of witnes- sing the full prodaction each afternoon at two. •
"Cinderella" is a triumph in many re- spects, for the company is a remaoably tal- ented one, the scenery is on "a: most generous scale, whilo the stagecraft is the "last word" in the art.

/Throughout the eleven scene S the show moves brightly and merrily. The drolleries of Harry Weldon, a clever and hardworking Buttons, keep the audience in =a constant roar. He works in perfect harmony with dainty Daisy Burrell, who captivates all with her bewitch- ing personality as Cinderella, and scores a big singing success with the "Broken Doll."
It would be difficult, too, to find a, more 4onalajg: ?riao•-; awn Ostia) Mayne. . Arthur
Aiston makes a capital Baron, and Bert Errol and Bert Byrne, as the Ugly Sisters, assist to provide most acceptable mirth.

The enchanted lake scene, where a number of girls enter the water—a huge tank is pro- vided in the stage—in search of the lost slipper is the most pleasing of many delightful scenes. "Cinderella" should break all records, for it is exceedingly well dressed, diverting to a degree, strongly musical, and good wholesome entertainment.

div.head: Great Circus at Liverpool Olympia.
div.p: Great Circus at Liverpool Olympia.
The Olympia, Liverpool, will this Christmas present the cream .of the circus profession in an entertainment in the ring, the like of which has never been seen in these islands before.

We shall find Jack Smiles clowning to the full bent of his humour; Grock and his part- ner, who will assuredly bA responsible for much unrestrained mirth; 'Paul: Gordon, an American humorist of high repute; and Eddie and Cornel, who introduce one of the funniest aerial acts ever seen.

At the head of the performing animal sec- tion will be found the wonderful Royal Assam troupe of elephants. Gardner's "Maniac" (quite harmless) Bulldogs and Terriers are an- other novelty: The wonderful donkey, "Tomato," belonging to the Decars, will in- trcxliice a troupe of trained geese. Bonita, the calculating pony, will do sums in arithmetic.

The riders and acrobats engaged are at the very top of the tree and include the Shannon Family, who, among other novelties, will in- troduce "Charlie Chaplin on horseback." And there are many other features.

div.head: BRIGHTER SIDE OF WAR.
div.p: BRIGHTER SIDE OF WAR.

During Monday and Tuesday morning motor ambulances transported loads of handicraft work from the various local hospitals to the Patten Hall, Winmarleigh-street, for exhibition and competition on Tuesday afternoon. With an enthusiasm born of desire for glory and prizes, for augmenting their Christmas festivi- ties fun, and for helping the British Red Cross Society, which has done so much for them, the wounded soldiers eagerly contributed their offer- ings of paintings, wood carving, and needlework made while held up in the sick ward. Of the making of handiwork by soldiers there is no end, and the several hundred specimens did them credit.

Almost all of a high order, the ,exhibits gave the judges pretty problems to solve. Fletcher and Mrs. Segar Owen; knit- ting, Mrs. Dakin and Miss Rylands. The peace kite that was flown last week. by Germany in-the name of herselfand her gentle Allies floated into official quarters in England in sufficient time to give Mr. LLOYD. GEORGE a magnificent opportunity at once to deliver his first speech as Prime Minister and to tell Germany what ,this country and her Allies think. of the kite. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE and his Government want peace; we all pine for it, and we are going to fight on to secure it the absence of certain conditions which do not appear to be forthcoming. The Germans, brazen-faced to the last, adopt high moral grounds in stating their reasons for propos- ing that we should enter into peace negotia- tions. But if there is one thing more ce;tain

than that we cannot trust ourselves to enter into agrfements, unbacked by the acknow- ledged superiority of our strength, with these super-criminals of the Prussian caste, it is that we cannot discuss humaneness with them. How can we discuss questions of humanity with the people who sank the 'Lusi- tania, and have since Made the sinking of innocent vessels a matter of wanton play? How can we join the ravagers of Belgium and the accessories to Turkish murders in Armenia by .the 'hundred thmiSand, in an effort to end the "atrocities of war " ? 'The pretence to serve a noble end is clearly a mask to cover some subtler impulse that has impelled Germany to make this move. Mr. Asounli, who roused the House to a state of marked enthusiasm by intimatiag that he in- tended to give the new Government the bene- fit of whatever experience he has gained, indi- cated, most probably, the true reason for Germany's new-found desire for peace. "The pronouncement, in my view," said the EX- PREMIER, and he knows the condition of Ger- many if anyone in this country does,," was born of military and economic necessity." No other reason is possible. It is altogether in- conceivable that Germans, who only a few short years ago were boasting of their abiftty and intention of being in Paris one month and London the next, should now be talking of peace except for the very good reason that they do not see their way successfully to make war.

In any case. they knew the terms upon which we were prepared to make,peace. They had been summarised by Mr. Asounn and Sir EDWARD GREY, and this week they, have been reiterated by Mr. LLOYD GEORGE and Mr. BONAR LAW. The terms are restitution,

reparation and guarantee against repetition of the wild beast work, of which Germany has been guilty. When Germany agrees to talk upon these lines we shall be ready for, peace; but, as Mr. LLOYD GEORGE declared, "mere words." such as lured Belgium to her dettruction will not satisfy Europe any more. In the name of the British Empire and our Allies he added that in the meantime "we shall put our trust in an ,unbroken Army rather than in a broken faith." Mr. Asounn expressed the same idea in another way, hut as emphatically. "Peace," he said, " will only come on: the terms that atonement is made for the past wrong and that paper treaties and the sovereignty of public law are securely entrenched among the nations of the world." We fear that Germany will not at present accept these conditions precedent to entering upon the negotiations for which she appears to be anxious. Up to now her rulers have come as victors with threats of further violence upon their lips. They know in their heart of hearts whether they are right, or Mr. AsourrH is right—whether they are anxious to save the World from 13uffering or 'whether they are in extreznis, militarily and financially. Our version of the situation' is that they have attempted the three-card trick upon perplexed neutrals and the confidence trick upon a doubting home population. It is in any case certain that so long as they arro- gantly pose as victors we cannot talk with
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1916.
them of peace. For the honour of our own times and the safety of our posterity we dare not. •

. „ Yesterday we' had some "proior that the three-card trick had secured one victim. PRESIDENT' WILSON, for some iinknoWn reason; has invited the belligerents to 'avow "their respective views as te the .terms upon which the war might be-concluded." Against the loudly proclaimed opinion on the part of the American people that Mr. LLOYD GEORGE had, taken the correct stand, their PRESIDENT only rushes in to second the suggestion of Ger.- many that negotiations shotil4 be opened. He tries to dissociate his action from that of Ger- many, but, to say the least, it is unfortunate that the two proposals should be separated by something less than a fortnight. Mr. WILSON is unfortunate in the reasons he gives for his suggested action. He says both sides have the'Same' object in view--to "mate the rights and privileges of weak peoples and small States as secure as those of great nations! That one sentence demonstrates Mr. WILSON'S incapacity to deal with the great issue into which he has recklessly thrown 'himself. Our answer to him will be identical: with -our answer fo Germany. We will talk of peace when Germany consents, or has been forced to consent, to make small nations as 'secure as great nations.

div.head: NOT PEACE. BUT A SWORD.
div.p: NOT PEACE. BUT A SWORD.
Christmas, 1916.

Though cravens clamour in the street With shrill premeditated cries; Though wind-blown politicians bleat Like sheep with colic, fed• with lies; Though sophists preach from day to day Their old pedantic shibboleth, The soldier sternly holds his way 'Unmoved. unfaltering at death. For 'mid the dust of ruthless war,
He. sees, and seeing steels his heart, The glory of the morning star, And like a hero plays his part. His soul instinct with steel and fire.
He sets his breast against the flood, And struggles onward through the mire, The flame of Freedom in his blood.

Behind the trend', beyond the strife, He sees, like pastures after rain, A nobler end, a richer life, A mighty people horn aga i n A people strong in deed and, will, Clear-sighted, iron-handed, free; And brooding over dale and bill, The Peace .begot of Liberty : , Even as a wayfarer may stand Where in the plain the tempest blows, And sees afar a rain-washed land • That brightly 'through the storm-cloud glows. Though his the life of field and tent. He has the prescience to see The vision fair, and, is content To fight or die for Liberty.

0 God of Battles, at Thy feet What precious wine of life is poured! What first fruits of untimely wheat Pall to tho harvest of the sword! Come Peace, not like a captive hound, That owns defeat, and shrinks from death, But like a Victor, laurel-crowned, Greeted as one that conquereth!

Come Peace beloved!, ,Not yet, not yet! But sterner hand-grip of the sword; God, steel our hearts lest we forget , , The righteous mandate of the Lord! 0 Christmas hells, your music cease; While cannons shake earth, sea and skies! We hail not yet the dawn of Peace, But tread the path of Sacrifice. • ALFRZ.Z. CARNEY.

HISTORY IN THE MAKING.
THE YEAR'S EVENTS, 1916
BY A WELL-KNOWN PUBLICIST.

Once more a year of war has to\ be recorded. Nineteen . hundred and sixteen ends, as it begin, with the Empire •engaged with its Allies in a great struggle of which the end is not in sight, though the enemy has called for peace. The area of the war has been ex- tended; its fierceness has .been intensified. The fundamental facts about it remain un- altered, and another year leaves Us with reso- lution strengthened and courage unimpaired. The list of nations at war is increased by the adhesion of Rumania and Portugal .to. the side of the Allies, and Italy has extended the scope of her responsibilities by declaring war on .Germany. A notable' -figure has passed off the European stage by the death of Franeis Joseph, Emperor of Austria, whose troubled reign since 1848 has ended amid world.: upheaval with the outlook.? black far. his, .country. This is the only toll that death has taken of the Thrones of Europe; but among humbler 'folk he has reaped -a terrible haryest, and one.-outstzinding name has been erased from among the Eying by the death of .Lord Kitchener. ;On June sth the cruiser Hamp- shire, on her way to Russia, struck a mine, and Britain lost her War Minister and her greatest soldier.

div.head: WESTERN FRONT.
div.p: THE WESTERN FRONT.

Fighting on the Western Front claims at- tention first, for, according to the prevailing but not unchallenged iiew, the really de- cisive theatre of war is there. And the story of the year is a cheering one of enemy failure and Allied success. The German effort was directed against Verdun, the fall of which, if it .had been achieved, would have been im- portant on Moral and: possibly dynastic grounds rather than from 'any great. strategic advantage. But' the Crown Prince main- tamed his tradition of incapacity, and the result, which an• ostentatious award of oak leaves does not obscure, has been a fright- fully costly failure. Very different is the story of the British offensive. In June we created, thanks largely to the gallantry of bhe Canadians, ,a diversion in the neighbour- hood of Ypres very serviceable to our French Allies. In the following month, after a can- nonade which may. be regarded as a triumph for our ' munition workers, we began the great, push. A great haul of prisoners her- alded a Movement that was well maintained through three stages, and in November, de- spite impediments created by the weather, there was a new advance. ,At the lessened pace necessitated by 'winter ' the offensive continues, and simultaneous counter-attacks by the French from Verdun make a welcome contribution. One feature 'of this fighting calls ,for special • mention. The false tradition of superior . inventiveness and) initiative on the part of • the enemy has received 'another blow by our introduction _of devastating ar- moured ears which, ,under the soldier's name of "_Tanks,' have • struck , the imagination of, the world, spread alarm amongst the enemy, and achieved results. of considerable, military value. There were staff changes on this front in the middle of December. General 'Tare, on be- coming General - in'- Chief of ''the - French' Armies and . Technical Military Adviser to the French GeVernment, ceased to 'be: reiponsible for the active direction of the French and British Armies in the field, and was succeeded by General Nivelle a soldier whose native talent has won hinif:- rapid promotion and great reputation in the present war.

div.head: EASTERN THEATRE.
div.p: THE EASTERN THEATRE.

- There are good and bad features in the re-' view of Eastern events. In the early days of the year wel completed our., evacuation of Gallipoli, and a special committee was later , , appointed, in reply to Parliamentary criticism, to consider all the. circumstances of an expedi- tion Of wkieh material for public judgment is lacking. The same course has been taken in the ease of the Mesopotamia campaign, where there was a serious breakdown in the, Medical arrangements for which -responsibility eas yet to be fixed. This campaign, which opened, as Xr. Asquith said, with exceptional promise, received a set back when. General Townshend's force was besieged in But-el-Amara, and after nearly 150 days of gallant resistance forced to yield to the ;lurks on April ,24th, before the relieving force could reach it. Our Russian 'Allies, still' hampered, though less than for- merly, by shortage of munitions, have done good work in the Caucasus, where the fall' of Brzeroum an Trebizond was a heavy blow to the Turks; .and, wheh better Weather made fighting on the main front possible in June, they conducted an offensive of which the great haul of prisoners and booty from the Austrians was a striking feature. Czernovitz, • Torno- 'poi, Lutsk, and Bolomea fell to our. Ally. Meanwhile,' Italy too was punishing Austria. The enemy thrust in, Trentino was a failure, and the initiative definitely passed to the Italians with the fall of CrOrizia. Rumania's entry at this point on the side of the, Allies drew the full force of enemy ttack upon her. Despite Russian ossistanco to the new Ally, the enemy has won Spectacular victories which, no doubt, had something, to do with the peace move in December. But the pro- ceeds in oil and grain were less than had been expected, and the results were secured by such a necessary drain on depleted forces that a final judgment on the military value of the venture may be' suspended-. In. November the Allies re-entered Monastir.

div.head: GREEK KING'S DUPLICITY.
div.p: GREEK KING'S DUPLICITY.

Balkan politics are allaays confusing, and. the treachery of the King's party in Greece has introduced a new element Of cotnplexity in the past year. It has been evident through- out that the Royalists have been intriguing with the enemy; and M. Venizelos, without definitely challenging the dynasty, set up a -Provisional Government; which the Allies have recognised as the de facto GoVernment where it has succeeded in asserting its authority. The position is admittedly anoma- lous, and it is not surprising that the conduct of our diplomacy has been rather obscure to the Early in December the situation became particularly grave. In spite of assur- ances 'given by the King, troops under Admiral Fournet were attacked in Athens, and the Allies had to take .strong measures. There was a show of refusal, but Constantine at - last capitulated. A couple of months earlier Admiral Fournet' had successfully' de- manded the handing over of the Greek Navy and large quantities of war material. A governing feature of Allied diplomacy has been the determination not to exploit the un- fortunate condition of ,Greece unscrupu- lously and without regard to the interests of the Greek people. Changes of Cabinet in Greece have occurred with striking rapidity, but without much effect.

div.head: NAVAL WAR.
div.p: THE NAVAL WAR.

The history of a year's work of Ole British Navy must not be sought in a euccession of sensational events. The security of our shores against invasion and the evident pressure of the blockade on the enemy have been the achievements of the Fleet. The latter, of course, involved a complex of naval and diplomatic considerations, and it was found advisable to set up a special Ministry of Blockade' which has been skilfully admin- istered by Lord Robert Cecil. One attempt was made to break the pressure. On May 81st the German High Seas Fleet sallied out and engaged the British Battle Cruiser Squadron under Admiral Beatty. An hour's ,action ended when the Grand Fleet, under Admiral Jellicoe, was sighted,. and the enemy made' off. Although we lost the battle-cruisers Queen- Mary, Indefatigable, and ,Invincible, the armoured cruisers Defence, Black Prince, and Warrior, and eight torpedo- destroyers, the balance was in our favour, though Ger- many, of course claimed a victory. "A few more such viCtories," cans, tfeally obsertied Mr. B ' alfour then First Lord of the Admir- alty, land. there will be nothing left of the German Fleet." An abortive Channel- raid and a 'raid on drifters off the Kentish coast completed the tale of Germany's naval action, property so-called. For the rest, she has r& lied oa the =glorious exploiter of her woke-

sea craft. Naval policy, meanwhile. has beet!, as usual, the subject of very t considerable controversy in this country. A Attiking con- tribution was made -to it early in the year by Mr. Churchill, who demanded the recall of Lord Fisher to the Admiralty. This speech was rather severely handled by Mr. Balfour, but changes todk place early in December by which Sir Henry Jackson ceased to be bbe First Sea Lord, he going to Greenwich, and Admiral Jellicoe succeeding him. The latter was, in turn, succeeded by Admiral Beatty in the command of the Grand Fleet.

div.head: =WAZMIIIM
div.p: =WAZMIIIM
ENEMY ".FRIGHTFULNESS.''

The submarine activities come more pro- perly under the heading of frightfulness. To Some extent our naval mastery has been limited by this new feature of maritime war- fire, and, in addition to such ontresges as the Sinking of the Italoja, a P. and 0. liner, with a loss of 155 lives, the Sussex, with a loss of 100 lives, and the mailboat Arabia—the last- named fortunately without loss of life—our food supplies have been menated. But confi- dence in the ability, of the Navy to grapple with the situation is general. The bravery of our merchantmen calls for •,special mention. scaptain Fryatt, a British skipper, was illegally executed fcir attempting to defend himselnagainst submarine attack, and the ease of Captain Blaikie at. the end of the year is in everybody's mind. The other branch of "frightfulness" has been conducted with the usual brutality, and military ineffectiveness - But the most satisfying feature of the air raids is that our defences appear now to have overcome the menace. In none of the last few raids has the enemy got away unscathed. Six Zeppelins were lost in three raids, and a daylight raid by aeroplane gave little promise of development along those lines. Nine per- sons were injured in London, )and the raider was brought down in France. But German barbarism has been seen at its worst in Belgium and Northern rrance, where "slave raids" have been made on the popula- tion revolting circumstances. A bogus "independence" was proclaimed for Poland to cover the attempted recruitment of Russian Poles to fight against their brothers.

div.head: IRISH TROUBLE
div.p: THE IRISH TROUBLE

Ireland, hailed at the outset of the war as " the one bright spot," has been Once more, the subject of controversy and disturbance. Fol- lowing upon a farcical escapade by Sir Roger Casement, who, after attempting to seduce prisoners of war from their allegiance in Ger- many endeavoured to land arms in Ireland, rebellion broke out in Dublin on Easter Mon- day. , This was the culmination of Sinn Fein activities, and Mr. Birrell, the Chief Secre- tary, _confessed that he had under-estimated the strength of this movement. His resigna- tion followed naturally, and the rest of the Irish Executive resigned with him. As a mili- tary manceuvre, the seizure of the Post Office and chief streets was little more than panto- mimic; but there were 794 civilian casualties, and many of the Sherwood Foresters lost their lives. The sequehe of the sorry business have aggravated feeling. There were 1,800 rebels executed, imprisoned, and deported. 'lames Connolly, Joseph Plunkett, P. H. Pearse, Thonms MacDonagh, Thomas J. Clarke, and J. Mcßride were among those executed, and the wretched Casement was -convicted or treason, degraded from his knighthood, and hanged. Following Mr. :Asquith's visit to Ireland, it was felt, that the opportunity had arisen for placing Irish Gov- ernment on a new basis. Mr. Lloyd George took in hand the task of reconciliation.' Lard Selborne resigned from the Government, ia Lace of proposals to apply Home Rule during the war. But the scheme was unworkable. Its basis was partial exclusion of Ulster' and there was no agreement whether this. should be temporary or permanent. So it broke down, and the .old order was set up again, with Lord Wimborne as Lord-Lieutenant and Mr.' Duke as Chief Secretary. A series of t illegal :executions, of which. Mr. Sheehi- Sieffington's case was the most notorious, added to-' the difficulties of the case.' A. judi- cial inquiry found Captain Bowen -Colthurst guilty of murder, while insane, 'in these cases. Inquiry has revealed the ,main external fea- tures of the affair, but the deeper causes are subjects • of -controversy. , The. Nationalist Party, which has always deplored the rising, blames' English harshnle. The treatment of prisoners and continuaCce of martial law re- main ' grievances; but there has been consider- able relaxation, and, in spite of bitterness a new and -better spirit is evident in all Irish parties, and there are vague but persistent rumours of an impending "settlement." '

div.head: POLITICAL PERTURBATIONS.
div.p: POLITICAL PERTURBATIONS.

Political disturbances culminated in Decem- ber in the fall of the Coalition Government. Its life had been a. series of crises, but it had turned many awkward corners, notably the transition from voluntaryism to conscription early in the year.. Lord Derby's report showed a great need for men, and it was held that the only way to secure them consistently with a pledge Mr. Asquith had given to married meu was to compel enlistment of the single. Sir John, Simon resigned from the Government, and led a vigorous Parliamentary opposition, while misgivings in the Labour World threat- ened the withdrawal of the Labour Members from the Cabinet. But national unity over- came all obstacles. The further conscription of the married followed in May, after another crisis and a secret session, and a proposal to compel youths of eighteen and time-expired soldiers, which Parliament emphatically re- jected. A couple of months later, Mr. Lloyd GeOrge succeeded Lord Kitchener at the War Office and Mr. E. S. Montagu became Minister of Munitions. Registration has pre- sented a still unsolved problem. The inherent weaknesses. of a Coalition became evident as the year advanced. There were clearly " fightings within" as well as without, and finally 3511- Lloyd George presented his scheme for a revolution in constitutional practice which has been generally regarded as an ulti- matum. Either he or Mr. Asquith had to go. The decision of the Unionists to support Mr. George was a. deciding factor. Mr. Asquith resigned, and, Mr. Law declining the Premier- ship, a Ministry was formed' by the ex-Secre- tary for War. Its chief innovations are the reduction of the Cabinet to five members— Mr. George, Lord Curzon, Lord Milner, Mr. Henderson, and Mr. Boner Law—the exclu- sion- of the principal •departmental chiefs, and the introduction of business men hitherto un- known to politics into the Government. The Liberal ex-Ministers have gone. into regular but friendly Opposition 'under Mr. Asquith, who has been reaffirmed as Liberal Leader. Sir Edward Carson, who resigned from the Coali- tion Government on the Eastern question, is now First Lord of the Admiralty, Lord Derby is War Secretary, and. Mr. Balfour is at the Foreign Office. The contact of the executive with Parliament has been greatly reduced, and the attitude of Parliament to the new order may be expressed in terms of the old one as "wait and see."

div.head: PEACE OFFER.
div.p: THE PEACE OFFER.

• In the midst of these events, and possibly encouraged by a misreading of them, came the German Chancellor's offer of peace from Central Europe to the Allies.. The demand for peace in Germany was obvious, but as the spirit of the offer implied a German victory, and ignored the great principles at stake in the war, it was recognised everywhere as unac- ceptable. "Adequate reparation for the past and adequate security for the future" were reaffirmed by Mr. Bonar Law, in Mr. As:- quith's words, as the demands of the Allies. That was the view widely taken abroad, particularly in America, where the chief ex- citement of .the year has been the Presidential election, resulting in the return of President Wilson, whose opponent was Judge Hughes. So the end of the year finds us still engaged in our great but net appalling task. That it is taxing the resouices of even the richest nation in the world is obvious. The total cost of the war up to December 16th was no less than 1:3,862,000,000.• But the nation is prepared to bear the strain until ;the. task is completed. :Lord Devonport, who holds the novel 0630 of Food Controller,' has foreshadowed con.- siderable additions to the existing interfer- enoes with the normal life of the people. White bread has been banished from our boards, and meatless days loom shoed. But, coine what come may," the"traiaitiOnil el Britons will be eaual• to the *maim. •

div.head: BOYS IN TROUBLE.
div.p: BOYS IN TROUBLE.
Stole Two Rifles To Go Poaching.

On Wednesday, at the'Lymm Petty Sessions, before Messrs. A. Watkin (in the chair), W. Peter Rylands, John Coxon, S. W. Gould and F. Lorkyer, two lads named Alfred Forsyth (17) and Harry Cadman (15) Were charged with stealing two rifles, valued at £5 each, the pro- perty of Mr. Thomas Frederick Dixon, Cliff- lands, Lymm. Superintendent Sutherland prosecuted, and Mr. Fieldhouse, solicitor, Manchester, repre- sented Forsyth. Both prisoners pleaded guilty. Mr. Dixon said that the two rifles, produced, had been in a motor car shed close to his back- door. On Thursday, 7th December, the door of the shed was locked. Early next day it was found that the lock had been forced and the rifles taken. The defendants had no right to take the rifles.
Sergeant Davies said that on the 9th Decem- bv he saw the defendants at Mni Gibbon's farm, where they were employed. Cadman adt

!flitted having laken the 'rides and said they were hidden in the hayjoft at the farm. He also said that Forsyth kot a screwdriver, took the lock off the motor shed door and threw it into the canal. Forsyth said "Yes, but he showed me the way." By Mr. Fieldhouse : He knew the boy For- syth, to be an epileptic. He had fallen into the canal on one occasion.

Mr. Fieldhouse, addressing the Court oire be- half of Forsyth, said this was no ordinary attempt at theft, but was with the object of poaching. the boy Forsyth was approached by a person in the village—the. manager of an establishmenti—whO said to him: "You are living in the country now and you will be able to get me a few rabbits and hares and I will buy them off you." The boys conceived the idea of poaching and they went and took these guns. If there had not been the pros- pective receiver of the game these boys would ,not have done what they did. it was a case of the older mind suggesting to the younger. The boys actually went into the village to buy cartridges, a fact which showed that they never intended to make money out of the theft.

' Mr. Forsyth, called -by Mr. Fieldhouse, stated that his boy was subject to epileptic fits since he was 154 years old and was most im- pressionable to suggestion. The magistrates retired to consider their decision, and the Chairman said they consid- ered that Forsyth had been under the influence of the boy Cadman, and ho would be bound over in .25 to keep the peace for 12 months, and to be visited at different intervals during that period by the Police Court Missionary. In the case of Cadman it was fortunate ftir him that he did not come under the new Act, which would operate from the Ist January next, as the magistrates would have ordered him to Liverpool for a flogging. He would be fined 10s. and ordered to enter into the same" bail as the ,former defendant and•-to be kept under the rervision of the Court Missionary.

div.head: PUBLICAN FINED.
div.p: PUBLICAN FINED.
Drunken Customer Overcome On Cobbles.
At the Lymm Sessions, on Wednesday, Robt. Parker, licensee of the Spread Eagle Hotel, Lymm, was charged with permitting drunken- ness on his licensed premises on the 24th of November, 1916. _ _
Mr. Leicester Caldecutt, solicitor,-Knutsford, prosecuted on behalf of the police, and, 'Mr. Percy Jordan, of the firm of Messrs. Boclding: ton and Jordan, Manchester, appeared for Mr. Parker.

Mr. Caldecutt said that on this Friday even- ing a man named Moody and another man named Clark went into the Fleece Hotel, Lymm, about 8 o'clock and had two pints of beer. They remained there about half an hour and then proceeded to defendant's establish- ment, where they sat from 8.30 until 10.30. While there they were supplied with two whiskies each. Under the Liquor Control Board Order intoxicating drink could not be served after 9.30, but these men remained on. It was not suggested, however, that they were supplied with drink after that hour. Imme- diately after they left the house the man Clark fell.down on the cobbles. Moody saw that he was 'drunk and tried to lift him up. A Mr. and, Mrs. Johes, who were passing, saw his condition, and the former would state that he was helplessly drunk. At the top of Eagle Brow Clark fell' again, and Sergeant Davies came on the scene. Clark's wife, who came Along, refused to take her husband home,. and he was brought to the Police Statioh. The question was: Did the landlord permit drun- kenness on his premises? -Sergeant Davjes saw lir. Parker the following day and the latter 9.sked what sort of man Clark was. When witness described him, defendant recognised the description and said Mr. Moody and he had two whiskies and that Moody said he would see Clark home. As a matter of fact, the men lived in different directions Moody at Limm-lane Crossing and Clark at Statham. From the Fleece to the Spread Eagle. Charles Moody, examined, said that he and Clark had two pints of beer in the Fleece Hotel and then went to the Spread Eagle. Mr. Parker served them with two whiskies each before 9.30. They stopped in the house some time lOnger and witnesa had a lemonade. When they came out about 10.15 Mr. Clark fell in the strget and pulled witness down on top of him. He corroborated the statement of the solicitor for the prosecution as. to what took place afterwards. Cross-examined by Mr. Jordan, witness said he considered Mr. _Clark to be, quite sober while he was in the Public-house. They were both sober. They had two glasses of whiskey each

Mr. Jordan: The whiskey is not very string nowadays? Witness: A bit fiery. (Laughter.) In furthee cross-examination, •witness said that until Clark had got to the door he had not the faintest idea that he was drunk and he was very much surprised at what happened. He did not think he was drunk. He knew that for five or six weeks past Clark had been suf- fering from the' effects of a very bad dose of double pneumonia. He had been attended by Dr. Burrowes. of Lymm, and witness knew that the attack had left him in a very weak condition. , Ile had heard .that Clark had col- lapsed several times even during his work. - Mr. W. H. Jones, clerk, Bridgewater-street, Lymm, stated that when passing along the street with his wife about 10.30 he saw Clark lying on the roadway and the previous witness, could not manage him. He assisted in lifttig Clark on to the footpath and he considered that the latter waS dead drunk. He .smelled very stiongly of whiskey. _ _ _ _
14- Mr. -JOrdan: Ile -considered that Clark had taken a,lot of drink.

Sergeant Davies stated that from information he received he went to Eagle Brow about 10.40 o'clock and found the man, John Clark, joiner, in a helpless condition. In his opinion he was drunk. When witness was taking him to the Police Station Clark's wife came along and he offered to Id her take him home. She, however, thought It better that he should be brought to the Police Station. Witness saw Mr. Parker next day and the latter said that when, the two men were leaving the house Moody said: "I will see him hope." Witness pointed out that Moody lived at Lymm Cross- ing and the other at Statham, and Mr. Parker replied: "If he collapsed I cannot help it; they were quite sober when they left here." Mr. Jordan: You, don't suggest that Mr. Moody was drunk?—Well, he is not charged. You say that Clark was drunk?r-From what T could see he was drunk.
Sergeant Griffiths corroborated this evidence.
Did the Licensee Know ?

Mr. Jordan, for defendant. said, his client was not sumwoned for selling drink to a drunken person, but for permitting drunken- ness, and he submitted .that he .could not be convicted on this charge in the absence of ptoof of knowledge, connivance, or careless- ness. He argued that Clark's condition when he got,outside the public-house was due to the effects of the very serious illness from which he had recently suffered. Mr. Parker had been twelve months in charge of. the Spread Eagle and had formerly managed a house in Salford. He had been previously in the employment of the Refuge Insurance Company and retired on pension after twenty years' service.

Mr. Parker, in gi;-ing evidence, said that he had never , seen :Clark before the evening in question and only knew Moody slightly. He did not detect any signs of drink on the men when they came in and they behaved properly all the time they were there. They got two glasses of Nyhiskey and they each had a mineral water afterwards. He saw them go out and Clark was then sober.

By Mr. Caldecutt : There was nothing about Clark to indicate that he was either ill or drunk when he was in the house. Both men were talking to a Mr. Lawrenson about a house which had been to let. A Mr. Leah gave evidence as to the illness— double pneumonia—from which Clark had suf- fered, and Mr. Lawrenson, who saw and con- versed with him and Moody about 9.45, said he had no suspicion that 'either of them was under the influence of drink.

In this case, the magistrates having con- sulted in their private room, ' Mr. A. Watkin, (chairman) said they were unanimously of opinion that there must be a conviction. Mr. Parker would be fined £2 2s. and he would have to pay £2 2s. advocate's fee and 14s. witnesses' expenses. A sequel followed when John Clark, joiner, was put forward, charged with being drunk and _incapable on the occasion mentioned. . Sergeant Davies gave evidence and defendant admitted the offence, adding that he only had two pints of beer and two glasses of whiskey. A fine of ss. was imposed.

div.head: URBAN COUNCIL.
div.p: URBAN COUNCIL.
hy The Tribunal Chairman Resigned.

Councillor F. Lockyer presided at the monthly meeting of Lymm Urban Council on Thursday. There were also present Councillors J. H. Holt (vice-chairman), W. G. Groves, R. H. Gotobed, F. • Ingham, A. Mclntyre, S. Critchley, T. H. Warburton, C. E. Cowper, and G. H. Parker, with Mr. W. Mullard, clerk. . Tribunal Chairman 'Resigns.

Mr. T. J. Ridgway, chairman of the• local Military Tribunal, 'wrote: "I much regret to. have to resign my appointment as a .member of the local Tribunal. I am only taking this step after most careful consideration, and feeling that I cannot attend to my duties as I should wish. I also wish to hank the Council for hav- ing appointed me a Member of the Tribunal."_.

eat;ticillor Gotobed said that they were all very sorry to receive that letter. Those of them who were members of the Tribunal and had the privilege of sitting under the chairmanship of Mr. Ridgway, knew how much they would lose by his resignation. By his'great tact, Mr. Ridg- _

div.head: TO PRODUCE FOOD.
div.p: TO PRODUCE FOOD.
WHespread Desire For Allot-
merits.
COUNCIL'S SUPPORT.

Mr. W. Mclntyre took the chair at TueA3- day's meeting of the Stockton Heath Parish Council and a question of absorbing interest was raised when Mr. Edwin Bradshaw (clerk) announced that he had received communica- tions in connection with a proposed allotments scheme. _ _

' One correspondent, Mr. S. Battersby, wrote applying for an allotment of land "under the new Order." The following letter was also received from Mr. E. G. White, eeeretary of the Stockton Heath Garden Society :—" At a meeting of my committee last week it was unanimously resolved that our society was wholly in favour of the provision of allotments in the village and would be prepared to co- operate or assist in any way with your Council for the furtherance of the movement for the growing of food, not only as a temporary, but more especially as a permanent institution for the district."- _ _

• Mr. Westbrook did not think that the new Order applied to Parish Councils. Mr. Clarke: The first thing we ought to do is to grow vegetables during the war. The Chairman: Mr. Battersby has particu- larly emphasised the fact that if he is granted land he wants it near his own house. (Laugh- ter.) He thought there was some available in Alexandra-road. The whole question is one of financing the scheme. Mr. Rose said that in view of the new in- structions from the Board of Agriculture .it was thought that public authorities should take up the scheme. He explained that on the previous evening a meeting of people interested in the allotment question was held in the Adult School, when it was decided to form an Allotment Association. for Stockton Heath and district, 'but it had nOthing to do with the Parish Council. Mr. Colenutt, of the Agricul- tural Organisation Society and the local secrt- lary of the North-Western 'Division, addressed the meeting and pointed out the necessity of making the movement a permanent one. He (Mr. Rose) was appointed secretary of the asso- ciation' thus formed, and he had bad already 26 applications for allotments. It was thought that the ,Parish Council could assist them in the matter by suggestions. The movement had nothing to do with the recent war instructions: and, in fact, applications for allotments had been made before the instruction was received. The allotments were wanted as a permanency. Inapplicable Regulations.

Mr. Westbrook thought that the new regu- lations only referred to County Councils and Urban District Councils. ile did not think they applied to Parish Councils, or even to Rural District Councils. - _ _

Mr. Bottomley said the Parish Council had a power as regards allotments, but .they should consider the question as to whether there were any landowners prepared to grant land for allotments. If Sir • Gilbert Greenall thought fit to let a certain quantity of land at a rental for allotment gardens there was nothing to stop him, and they could, as a Council, make a suggestion to Sir Gilbert or any other land- owner in the district and ask him if he was prepared to. do so. There was nothin to pre- vent Mr. Rose from asking -Sir Gilbert if he was prepared to let off portions of his land for the purpose of growing produce. They had, as a Council, no power to deal with the ques- tion of allotments unless they adopted the Small Holdings Act. Mr. Westbrook quite agreed. As a Parish Council they would not be justified in going to any expense. If they were going to do any- thing in the way of allotments they should do it legally by first adopting the Act. Mr. McDermid said the 'general opinion at the meeting of the Garden: ,Society was that the scheme- should be a permanent one and he thought the Council should give whatever sup- port they could in the effort to obtain land for allotments.
Mr. John Hallows also urged the support of the Council to the movement.

It was ultimately decided, on the motion of Mr. Westbrook, seconded by Mr. Bottomley, "That this Council has heard with pleasure of the formation of the Allotments Associa- tion and of its efforts to obtain land for the purpose within the parish." It was pointed out that the moral support thus given to the• project by the Council would hasten the realisation of this admirable scheme. ,

The Education Committee decided to support! the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Insti- tutes in their demand that no exemptions, either partial or whole, shall be granted to children under fourteen years of age; and that educa- tional facilities shall be given, in the daytime for young people between the ages, of fourteen and eighteen. To allow of the latter arrangements the sug- gestion is that employers shall give six hours a week " within the ordinary hours of employ- ment" to their young people. Mr. John Upson, who moved the resolution, said no words were required .to commend the resolution to the committee. Alderman. Bennett was of opinion that the time was fully ripe for taking the step. It was manifestly unfair that the children of the poorer , classes should have a worse education than others. It would be of great advantage to them to go to school longer, and .when they 'left be able to leave work for a •few hours in the day time in order to have lessons in school. Why should the poor little beggar's have to work. all day, and then go to night school? He some- times thought that their physical development was apt to. he retarded' in that way. Whilst agreeing with-the resolution. Council- , lor Wilson pointed out that owing to industrial conditions many parents had hard work to keep their children, and if they were to stay at school longer means should he fciun& to feed them. He instanced the ease of a soldier who was apply- ing for his child to leave school at 13 years of age. "I don't want him to leave school,", said the soldier, "but what can I do? I have only my paltry pension and cannot support him." A good education should be given children with- out any Ainancial loss to them.

div.head: WHO IS RESPONSIBLE?
div.p: WHO IS RESPONSIBLE?

Since certain illuminative properties in thc Corporation 'gas have been extracted for the use cif the Government the ordinary burners employed in the Parochial School, Church- street, have failed to provide sufficient light. and. as the afternoons have worn on and. darkness has set in, considerable inconvenience has been caused both to teachers and scholars. • Edmund Burke once said that "*Darkness is more productive of sublime ideas than. light" —but, one adds, the learning of the three R's cannot be done in the shadows. When the . light of nature fails and that from primeval gas burners fails to ,make up the leeway, in- Candescent fittings, in the absence of electric lamps, are required. This urgency is recognised both by the school •' managers and the Education Committee, but as to who should bear the expense there is much dispute. In a blaze of electric light the Education Committee, sitting in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Monday evening, considered the matter. It was an illuminating discussion. • The Sites and 'Buildings Committee reported that a letter. had been received from the man- agers of the schooly asking them to provide incandescent lighting, but the sub-committee , could riot see their way to accede to the re- vest. The Chairman of the Sites and Buildings Committee, Mr. R. T. Fairclough, who is also a manager of the Parochial School. disagreed - with the recommendation of the committee, remarking that it was an injustice both to the teachers and the scholars. as well as to the managers. Before the war the lighting was good enough, but owing to certain properties in the gas being taken out, it was too bad now for the work of the school to be carried on efficiently. Under the circumstances, he thought the Education Committee ought to provide new fittings. If the managers were .left to do so the town would get all the bene- fit, as .the gas consumed would he less— entirely due to the provision of incandescent fittings by the managers. Alderman Tinnion believed that Mr.. Fair- dough was the only 'member of the committee who-was against the refusing of the application. ' Gas fittings were part of the structure, and should, therefore, be paid for by the mana- gers. The lighting in the school was tv. dis- grace to the managers. Before certain illum- inative powers- of the gas supplied were ~ext- racted it was inefficient. He had been to recruiting meetings and the men who re- sponded could scarcely see to sign, their names. Alderman Smethurst thought that the man- agers should help, as, nowadays, it was par- ticularly hard fOr .voluntary school managers to obtain the money to run the schools. • • Is The Education Committee Selfish?

The Rev. Father Hind supported Mr. Fair- dough and remarked that it was a most im- 'portant matter as to who was responsible for the lighting of the schools. The lighting in his (Father Hind's) own schools was something appalling at the - present and he had had to pay for it tO be -altered in the one; he Could not do so for the two of them. By managers • providing the special incandescent fittings they ' were saving the Education Committee consid- ' erable expense, not only in that way, but by reason of the less quantity of gas consumed, 1 that being provided by • the Corporation. In- cidefitally, the speaker declared that on com- , ing to Warrington he found that managers of - denominational schools were saddled with greater financial responsibilities than in any other town he knew. Mr. C. H. Unsworth was also on the side of ' Mr. Fairclough. . In reply to Mr. John Upson. the. Chairman (Councillor Henry Roberts) said the legal aspect of the position was not very clearly. defined. In order to test the feeling of the commit- tee, the Rev. G. C. Briggs moved, 'and Mr. George Walker seconded, that the minute be referred back. / Councillor Firth Lindley contended that gas fittings were part of the school structure and should be paid, for by the managers. The present lighting arrangements had been in existence for over twenty years and should have been altered long ago. Alderman Tinnion entirely and facetiously agreed with Councillor Lindley, adding that the lighting was so bad that blind man's buff was the only occupation that could be pro- perly indulged in there. (Laughter.) Councillor J. T. Locker: May I take it that no school has been furnished with special lighting by the Education Committee except- ing those used for evening classes? Alderman Tinnion: That is so. Councillor Locker said that, as a manager, he might mention that whatever the outcome of that discussion, the lighting arrangements would have to be altered. In these days it was very difficult to get money for denominational schools. Mr. Upson wondered whether the additional lighting was part of the payment of the privi- leges allowed denominational schools .or not. Is The Corporation Morally Responsible? • The Chairman: There is one point: the lighting of the school prior to the war was, I don't Isay satisfactory but sufficient to pass the requirements. The Corporation has, in conse- quence of the war, now extracted something from the gas which has made it poorer. It seems to me that it is a question of equity as ! to whether the difference in lighting should be . made up by the Corporation. The Vice-Chairman (Mr. A. J. Jolley) first replied to the Rev. Father Hind by stating that, as a manager of a voluntary school and knowing the difficulties besetting them, the local authorities had always dealt generously with them as far as the law permitted, and if other towns had been more generous by going beyond the law that wiis no reason why War- rington should follow suit. He supported the recommendation of the committee. Mr. C. E. Parker thought it was the legal aspect of the position that required to be decided. He did not think there was much in the point raised by Mr. Fairclough about the present deficiency of the lighting, because .he had attended meetings there and the lighting was always bad. While Mr. Parker was speaking the Chair- an interposed With the remark that unless one bad incandescent mantles one could not read by the gas provided in Warrington. - Mr. Parker: I have incandescent fittings and even then cannot read by .it. (Laughter.) ' Mr. Fairclough mentioned that the 'cost would be about X2O. It was decided to refer the minute back for further consideration.

"MODERN WITCHES."
Amazement Caused By Their
Exposure.
SPIRITUALIST SOCIETY'S
DISCLAIMER.

"The Examiner's" exposure of Warring- ton fortune-tellers in laid week's issue was read with great interest. It caused consider- able discussion generally and alarm in the quarters described. Almost needless to say, the Spiritualist Society, who have sent the following letter, were not alluded to, nor even in our minds, when the article was written.

div.head: To the Editor of "The Examiner."
div.p: To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—l read with some amazement your article in last Saturday's " Diaminer " under the above heading. Not having the opportu- nity of attending our Police Courts, and never having visited one of the local " wizards" (-?." witclies "), as I should not know where to find one, I was surprised to read that there were so many in our town. I have heard vague rumours of such persons, but never any- thing definite. Still, one thing puzzles me, and that is-.--if this is such an objectionable practice, how is :it that at almost every bazaar either for church funds or for charitable ob- jects one of the attractions is a lady "palmist" —as, for instance, at the Naval Day Fete— whose sanctum is crowded with those curious to .know whether anything relating to the future can he indicated to them. No doubt,

_ many go just for the fun of the thing, but in. others the spirit of curiosity is awakened within them, which is calculated to make them like Nicodemus, and visit these people surreptitiously. I'do not wonder at the num- ber of clients some of these women have; especially at this time, when so many hearts are oppressed with Anxiety and dread. As representing the local Spiritualist Society, I wish. to .say that we entirely and strongly deprecate and discountenance this fortune-telling practice, and there is not, se far as I know, a single member of our body, either male or female, who opens a house for the reception cif .visitors of the class -referred- to in your article. If there is, and it can be privately proved to me, I should be glad to receive the information, so that we may know how to deal with them. . I make a distinction (which the -law does not) between genuine _ _ .

mediumship for spiritual guidance to those in need of it and the debasing practice referred to by your contributor. Our main object as an organisation is ,to " prove" what the churches only preach—the continuance of life after the death of the body, and also the pos- sibility of tho actual communion here and now of our departed friends with those sth in the body.,—Yours, • WV. E. STOUT, President.. 33, Cairostreeti, Warrington.

Platelayer's Terrible Death At
Bank Quay.
RUN OVER BY TRAIN.

Engaged on an errand et comfort to his men, shivering in the fog of Saturday evening, a Well- known foreman 'platelayer was .knocked down and fatally injured by a train at Bank Quay, the refreshments he was carrying being scat- tered about the line: He was Samuel Faulkner, aged 56, of 59, Wakefield-street. The inquest Was conducted by Mr. S. Brig- house on Tuesday. Mr. I. Brassington, official of the National *Union of 'Railwaymen, and Mr. Georg Forster; of the Permanent Way Depart- ment, L. and N.-W. Railway, were present. , Mrs. Sarah Faulkner said she saw her hus- band at the Infirmary. He was conscious and, . pointing to his left side, said, " This leg is off." ; On Sunday morning about one o'clock she again went to the Infirmary arid stayed with him until his death at 6.25 a.m. Charles ,Henry Dutton, foreman shunter, stated that at twenty-five minutes Past eight on Saturday evening he was on the. up side plat- form at Bank Quay Station. The, 6.10 train from Liverpool. Which was late, ran into, the station, and a ‘passenger who had travelled on the train reported that he had felt the carriage give a jerk, as if something had been run over, a little way back along the line. -Witness went along the line and found Faulkner lying on the four-foot way. Ho was shouting and struggling, and witness saw that 'his left leg was off from the top of the thigh, and lying about .two yards away from him. His right foot was also -cut off. Witness shouted for assistance; they ban- daged him up as well as they could, and took him to the 'lnfirmary. When 'witness 7 found Faulkner the later was quite conscious, and said, " Billy, I. didn't think I Would have to come to this." Witness was known amongst the men as Billy. Faulkner was in charge of some men Who Were engaged along the line on fog- ging duty. He visited them during the night and at intervals took them 'refreshments. It was very foggy at the time, and witness saw the refreshments all scattered about. De- ceased was lying about 100 yards from the re- freshment room .and about •80 fro& the end of the platform. . The jury fannd that death was accidental, and tendered their sympathy to the widow and family. The Coroner said that the work of railway men was very arduous at the present time, and he had deep sympathy for them. . Mr. George Forster, for the Engineering 'De- partment, expressed their deep regret. D'eceaSed had been 33 years in the service of the company, and 26 year .as guard. He was an extremely . good servant and highly respected.

Many so-called weeds are, however, .still used by the medical profession, but when they figure on prescriptions they are dignified by learned atin mines. The dandelion enters into a number Of preparations, for it contains valuable medicinal properties. The various mints yield several kinds of essential oil, and from peppermint comes •menthol and mint camphor. Neather Lore. Mr. J.. C. Davies's •" Folklore of West and llid Wales" contains other interesting weather beliefs., some of which are common to various places in which I have lived.. It is "considered good. sign," for instance, "to see large num- bers of white ,butterflies." I met a lawyer in. the car, and he asked what I was reading. It was a lawyer who • asked Jesus 'Ault he must do to inherit eternal iife. The fiord said to him, "What is written in the Law? How readest thou?" That is a question xorth consideration still. I once. beard a ireacher deal with it, and he pointed out that the term "reading" had a much wider mean- ing than the perusal of books. Reading began tong before books were written. Men read the secrets of nature by studying land, sea, and ;Icy first hand. They perceived the' coming storm in the rising wind and the ink .black They read many of the mganings of ain, moon and stars. They saw food in ani- nals and fruits; and before books. were written the' ancients gave them the rudiments of nearly 111 the arts and sciences of to-day. As to lrinfed matter, Tennyson had only six favour- :te poets. They were Shakespeare, Chaucer, \Elton, Wordsworth, Dante, and Goethe. To pretend to do so is imposture of the most I,arefaced kind; to believe it is credulity of the grossest description I had almost paraphrased Paul's letter to the -Galatians, and added-0 foolish Warringtonians, who hath betwitched you? But of course the practices now depre- cated are common in all parts of the kingdom. Moreover, says Mackenzie—" Of many who sa3- they do not believe in .fortune-telling, I have known few on whom it had not a very sensible effect." Victims I Have Known.

Yes, indeed, rich and poor are equally de- luded. An old acquaintance of mine who lately passed away confided to me that, on account of a serious internal malady in relation to whicb. he had vainly suffeAd many things of many physicians, he had gone twice to Blackpool specially to consult a reputed wise woman— professional, of course. the consultations in volving substantial fees. In East Lancashirf I had a neighbour who was a cotton mill manager, and desired to commence business or his own account. His wife insisted that h( should go to Bacup and inquire of a famous fortune-teller there. He did so, and the woman warned him not to embark upon the contem• plated enterprise. He and three partners wen' on with the scheme, however, and although they did not make much money, it could hardly be pronounced a failure. His u)ife happened to think differently, and the poor fellow had therefore to endure much heaviness. When 1 was in Southport, where wealthy widows most do congregate, there was one artful fortune- feller in particular who flourished exceedingly by attending them at their own homes. It is all very pitiable and humiliating, and one cannot help feeling sorry for Warrington girls who have come within the toils of ti nch con- scienceless humbugs. One especially likes to see the police taking action against imposters of this class, and the Bench inflicting adequate penalties. Chestnuts.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1916.
DALLAM AND BEWSEY.
Manager's Praise And Advice
-At Annual Dinner.
"JOIN YOUR UNION."
"The elite of the ironworkers of Great Britain."

That -eulogistic phrase was one of the many used -by Mr. C. E. Bunch, works manager, to 100 representative men • from Dallam and Bewse.Y Forges • who assembled in the Lion Hotel on Saturday evening under the chair- manship of Mr. John T. Walker, to enjoy their annual dinner. • Along with • the Mayor (Alder- man Peter Peacock) and Mr. Jabez Hall, presi- dent of the Associated Iron and Steel Workers of 'Great Britain, Mr. 'Bunch was a guest of the men. The diners included several em- ployes in khaki (home on leave), managers and principals of departments. The loyal toasts hating been honoured on the initiation of the Chairman, Mr. Walker made an interesting speech, in which he declared that the reputation of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron C 0..; Ltd., had even been in- creased during the war, and it was second to none, (Applause.) What men could be spared had joined the Forces and had gone willingly; there were no 'conscientious objectors among them. (Laughter and applause.). In proposing the toast of "His Majesty's Forces," Mr.- W. llipkiss -greatly praised the Work of the Army and Navy, and spoke highly of those -employes of Pearson and Knowles who had rallied -to the Colours, and who were ready to bear privation, strain and discomfort in order that -England's honour and the rights of smaller nationalities might he maintained. He coupled the name of the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) with the toast. Lieut. Chilton was to have been present, but he was detained by pres- sure of work at headquarters. The toast having been honoured,

The Mayor responded, remarking that he was very proud that he was the first Mayor, who had ever been invited to attend their social gather- ing ,and he was pleased to find himself • not amongst strangers, but amongst friends. • Among the ironworkers of Warrington he counted his strongest supporters,. as in all the elections he had fought they had worked strenuously on his behalf. In this war Warrington had sacrificed some of her most gloriouti sons, and although Warrington had not so many men in the Navy as in the Army, those who had joined were men of grit and determination. Ironworkers at the present day were as essential as soldiers and sailors, in order that victory 'might be gained, for without.them there could be no vic- tory in the field. (Applause.) Mr. A. Smart proposed the toast. of the visitors, to which Mr. George Attwood and Mr. Cooke felicitously replied; the latter—who is secretary of the Works Charities Fund—urging
on all the men to contribute more than they had done, as tho institutions which they sup- ported were greatly in need of money.
PRAISE FOR EMPLOYES.

Scotsmen, have a toast to "The Town we live in." That fo "The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd.," proposed by Mr. H. Perks, might very well have been styled "The Firm we work for." Mr. Perks spoke highly of the company in its dealing with the men, and Pointed to the fact that he had never heard of there being a strike either at Dallam or Bewsey. They had a splendid set of managers from Mr. Bunch downwards. (Applause.) Replying to the, toast, Mr. Bunch said he was just as much pleased to meet his men round the festive board as he was to meet them in the .works. He was proud of them. ILL all sin-, ecrity, lie looked upon the men of the forges and mills With the greatest possible respect. " I am necessarily a lot amongst you," he added, "and, of course, I have occasion to talk with you. Sometimes our talk is of the robust, en- ergetic style, and sometimes it is quiet and dovelike—(laughter)--but we have been many years together and have become old and good friends, learning to look upon one another with a certain amount of confidence, and appreciat- ing one another's trials and difficulties. (Ap- plause.) Considering the size of the works, we have a minimum of friction, for a spirit of conciliation, co-operatidn and confidence has been developed between the management and the men." • Having urged the men to put forth all their strength in this critical time, Mr. Bunch said he was proud Of them, pnd was pleased to observe that only a few lagged be- hind in their duty.
Mr. Bunch had a good word for trade unions

"I earnestly desire that your union should be- come stronger every day," he declared. ." I should like all the ironworkers of Messrs. Pear- wn and Knowles to' become members of their own trade society. I speak like this, because I know my directors are just and reasonable, and because they and I would rather discuss im- portant trade questions with a united body than with individuals." Out of the various works associated with the company over 3,000 men bad joined the Colours, and many had made the supreme sacrifice. They all respected and honoured their memory—(hear, hear)—and must not have their glory besmirched by a peace which was dishonourable and un-English. (Applause.)

THE SAVINGS BANK'S PROGRESS.

That extravagance and wastefulness cannot be alleged of many of those earning high wages in Warrington may be deduced from the 'state- ments made at tho, annual meeting of the Warrington and Runcorn Savings Bank, held at the head office, Buttermarket-street, on Tuesday morning,

div.head: RECORD BUSINESS.
div.p: RECORD BUSINESS.

The Chairman (Mr. C. Jackson Holmes) had a happy story to tell regarding the thrift dis- played 'during the Fast year. In moving the adoption of the general statement if accounts. he said : " From a dissection of the accounts it is pleasing to find the number of depositors and the amount standing to their credit still mounting upwards. . There are now 19,810 ac- counts, an increase of 201 for the .year. The number of transactions is a record one and is due to the large increase (2,075) in the number of deposits, for there is a decrease of 1,187 in the number of • repayments, as compared with last year's totals. • This is very satisfactory, and no doubt duo to the fact that there is very little unemployment, work having .been plenti- ful and wages high; also to the fact that many are realising their country's needs :and are helping the Government to finance the war in a safe and most effective way .by depositing their small savings in the bank. A Big Turnover.

"The amount received from depositors, viz:, .2121.529, is also a record. one. There is a de- crease of ..e22.448 in the amount repaid to depositors, as against last year, notwithstandr ing the fact that ,P 19,505 h6s been paid out for the .purchase of exchequer bonds, the amount Paid to depositors being .2130,857. The turn- over now exceeds a quarter of •a million. " The ratio of the number of depositors to the inhabitants of .the district is nearly one in four. Your committee would be glad to see many more of the inhabitants taking advan- tage cf the facilities for the safe-custody of their small saving. Thrift is a virtue at all times, but it is absolutely necessary more of the people of this country should practice economy at these times, and at once begin to Put away some of their hard-earned wages. "During the year the new bank at Runcorn has been opened and is a handsome structure. It is quite a feature of High-street, and. when I tell you. that, there has been an increase since the amalgamation of over X 15,000 in the funds of that office I think you will agree that the amalgamation, which was advised by the

committee, was fully justified, and I may say further we have ' some very enthusiastic trustees and energetic managers at Runcorn; and, with such, a backing, I :predict that the bank will for many years fulfil the object for which it was established.

"Home safes still continue a popular means of saving small amounts. I should like to see more of these in use, as they are very valuable in encouraging the habit of thrift by securing the very smallest deposits and bringing them to the bank.

THE NEW MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Mr. Rowland Prothero is almost the first man of letters pure and simple to enter a Ministry. Ice does not belong to a political club, and he occupies one of those University seats which are practically non-political. His book on " ing" is the 'standard work on the political and historical side"of the subject, says "Farm and Home," but he will rely on the permanent offi- cials at the-Board of -Agriculture for the practi- cal issues of stockbreeding • and the: markets. The chief -interest in his appointment is in its reversing the Whole policy of the Board under the Marquess of Lincolnshire. Of the Small Holdings Scheme, with its tenancy as contrasted with a freeholding,. basis, and its compulsion as sk against State acquisition of land in the market, Mr. Prothero was known as the most erudite and damaging of critics. He is also a sworn foe Of waste land, and long before the war was urging the 'Government to reduce every Cultivable acre into up4o-date agricultural. use. It is one of the ironies Of the political situation and also it counts in every way to the credit of the Prime Minister, that be should have chosen for the appointment one of the bitterest oppon- ents of his financial and land policy. An even- ing -paper -regards it as one Of the 'strangest features of the new situation that Mr. Lloyd George, whose last pre-war activity, was the Liberal Land Campaign, should appoint to this post a foremost champion of that feudal land system which he set out to destroy.

div.head: WOMEN AND LADS ON THE FARM.
div.p: WOMEN AND LADS ON THE FARM.

The care of live stock takes a.„ foremost place in the various duties of the farm; and in these serious times it should be the first consideration. It is shortage of milkers that is threatening our milk supply almost as much as the dearness of food for the cows, and we must leave no stone unturned to train women and boys for that highly important work. An encouraging report CS regards women comes from Hertfordshire. The War Agricultural Committee have arranged for 2.000 women to work on 543 farms in that county, and milking and the care of stock form a largo part of their duties. If it be true, writes "Old Breeder," in "Farm and Home," that there are still parts of England where prejudice exists' against the employment of women, especially amongst stock farmers, they should be shown that women have proved them- selves quite capable in the rearing and, feeding of live, stock, • weaning lambs and calves in par- ticular, as well as being. the best of milkers. Another point which it is quite time to consider is the desirability of getting more boys on to the land. In the old days we used to employ them to drive the three-horse pleugli team at eight years, old. That might have been too young, but keeping them at school till they are four- teen seems a senseless waste of strength at such a time as this. All boys of thirteen should be unconditionally released without the formalities noW necessary. There is not 'much connected with cattle, sheep, pigs, and horses that a lad of that age could not do nearly or quite as well as men, and even better than some of their old grandfathers now at work.
