div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
LIQUID MANURE 1011 FRUIT TREES.

There are, I fear, many people who, having a surplus of liquid manure, do not turn it to advantage by feeding the fruit 'trees at this season .of the year. Now is the time to apply it, as the ground after the heavy rains we have had during November is now in fine condition for the liquid manure to benefit any trees that have borne a heavy crop of fruit, or where the soil is poor. When the liquid manure is Applied to soil that has been thoroughly moist- ened its fertilising properties are, as it were, held in suspense, and gradually filter down to the roots of the trees, and at once are available as plant food. A word of warning may, how- ever, be given here, and that is that it is a mistake to give liquid manure to young trees that are growing: freely, as such treatment only causes such trees to make a gross sappy growth that never ripens well, and consequently is all too often unfruitful. The asparagus bed, too, may well be given a share of any liquid manure that can be spared, as those who have had to dig up plants that have been in the same place for many years, know full well the number of roots and the depth to which they go in search of food. All too often the idea prevails that the winter is the wrong season to feed the trees in the way indicated, but if carried out at that season the benefit of the same will be apparent in the years that follow.

div.head: SWEET PEAS.
div.p: SWEET PEAS.

These are deservedly popular, and we . have now many varieties, so beautiful that they have been given separate names. w.hich we do not object to, provided they are quite distinct. This naming, however, has been carried to excess, as it cannot be denied that the difference in the shades ogf colour is in many cases so small that if several so-called varieties were placed together it would be very difficult, nay impossible;' to separate -them. There are a great many that are too much alike. Though we are always pleased to see and welcome anything distinct, and under a name by which we can •make sure of obtaining it, confusion is sure to follow if this naming is carried too far. Purchasers of seed of sweet peas prefer to have those varieties they can trust to be true to name and colour. In olden days this reliability .we used to have, but now chaos reigns, many of the varieties coming irregular and in all too many cases far from true to 'description. With not a few sweet peas fixity of character seems to be out of, the ques- tion. To my way of thinking no sweet pea should be put on the market until it has • been thoroughly tested. for at least three years. A trial of one year is quite unreliable.—" Wick," in " Farm and Home."

div.head: AN UNFRUITFUL PLUM TREE.
div.p: AN UNFRUITFUL PLUM TREE.

A correspondent writes me that he has in his garden a plum tree which grows very strongly, but that it never bears tiny fruit. This is evidently a case where root pruning is the only remedy. This is. best .done by taking ,out a

trench, 'say; three feet all round from the stem of the tree, and not less than two feet deep. Then when the soil has been removed all round gradually work in towards the stem and loosen the soil with a fork, carefully preserving all the. roots. When this has been completed go •over all the roots, and with a sharp knife cut off all the jagged and broken ends, and relay them carefully in the soil, with their ends point- ing in the surface. Should it be fOund that the soil is worn out then instead of returning the same replace it with some.good fibrous loam from an old pasture, and add some old mortar rubble if to be had. Should the mortar rubble not be handy, then a few bones will answer as well, but on no account use animal manure of, any kind, reserving this for laying on the surface as a mulch after the work has been completed. It may be found that as very often happens a tap root has found its way into the subsoil. If so, then it must be cut off close up to the bottom of the stem .and cleared away. In some cases treating one side of the tree as above advised may. check the over-vigorous growth, but if not then. the other side of the tree may be dealt with the following year. On no account prune hard, only thin the branches, as the root prun- ing will be quite sufficient to check the sappy growth and help to the formation of fruit buds.

It was fated De Vaux should not gain Paris for some time yet to come, nor alone. For, as the car sped swiftly through Mayfair it struck a taxicab with terrific force. Once' again the fatal gem for which Blair Stan- leigh and Vivian had schemed and striven, fought and robbed, had disappeared. With a deftness the result of long practice De Vans despoiled his un- conscious victim, and then running through the hall bolted the entrance door against Marmaduke and the footman who had been attending the post- man with the registered package. The respite en- abled the thief to regain the gallery and holding the diamond in his hand he dropped from the win- dow to the ground. Marmaduke was waiting for hint. The keen-witted lawyer had sensed a mur- derous attack, and as De Vans dropped lightly to the path he was tackled. From his hands flew the diamond, falling unnoticed into the lawyer's up- turned hat on the ground beside them. With a sickening pang at her heart ,Vivian real- ised there would be no pomp and ceremony for Blair, Earl of Stanleigh, and Vivian his fair Countess, to grace this day. Something of this must have passed through Blair's dulled aching consciousness. "Stop him! He struck me down! The diamond is gone!" He gasped, and fumbled at his bloodstained finery as he spoke. The Gothic window had closed back in place. Seemingly the armoured assailant had vanished as if by magic, only the heap of old mail accoutre- • //lents and helmet on the floorktold how the mur- derous intruder had hidden. The struggle at the back of the house was strenu- • ous but brief. . The -doughty lawyer was no match ' for the younger and -more muscular De Vaux. Throwing SmYthe aside and kicking at him I viciously, De Vault sprang to his feet and made off' just as the servants of Stanleigh House, followed by the Earl and his lady, came upon the scene. •Suspiciode and ever distrustful of Smythe, Blair refused to believe the lawyer had attempted to stay the mysterious assailant who had struck him down and borne away the diamond. Forgetting his grievous wound, and the blood that trickled down his livid face, Blair screamed hoarsely in his wild frenzy of anger and chagrin. "Pack your things," he shrieked. "You were in the plot; you were an accomplice, and I'll have your life for it!" Vivian paled. A chill went through her being. "Come, come," she whispered, tensely. "Come, dear, let us go into the house; you are badly hurt and the diamond is gone. Never mind, we will recover it. Everything will be all right—yes, everything will be all right." And for the first time in her wicked' life that- pity which is Ain to love filled her heart with a deep affecion. After all, wicked as he was. Blair Was a man, who had fought his way, unscrupulously and desperately it was true, but he had fought and.never whimpered—and for her!. Smarting under the unjust accusation of Blair, the lawyer stood absent-mindedly watching the Earl staggering back to the house. Then he placed his hat on his head, wincing as something dropped smartly' upon the skull, It was The Diamond from the Sky! Marmaduke put the jewel into his pocket, went into the house, and began packing up. In the midst of the operations Blair came into ' the room. "Pack up your things and get," he said, contemptuously. "Your own things and nothing but your own things, remember," snatching at the Hardings' family-tree parchment. A glance at the document and he flung it away. 'As your Lordship wishes," replied Marmaduke, dutifully, picking up the parchment. His bags were already packed, and he now shouldered the gun he had carried in America, and was turning to remove the deer head—the cherished souvenir of his second visit to the Yankee jungles—when Blair's exclama- tion, "Leave that alone." caused him to wheel around startled. The gun went off pointed back over Sinythe's shoulder, and the heavy charge of shot 'struck the deer head fair between the eyAs. The impact loos- ened whatever bound the deer head to the wooden mount; the deer head dropped forward, held at the lower part of the neck to the mount as though by a.hinge. A little puff of dust marked the break- away, and then from within the hollow neck a little package of yellow parchment, bound with faded tape, fell to the floor. , . .

Smythe picked it up and saw it was annotated in ancient angular writing, the ink faded to rust colour by age. The lawyer's eyes opened wide as he scanned the faded markings. " Herewithe Ye Marriage Lines of My First Wyfe Rachel Harding, A Gypsie Mayde, Who Bore Me A Son But Left Me In Dudgeon And Caste Off My Name Returning To Her Own 'People With Ye Childe, Nor Would She See Me More.

"(Signed) ARTHUR STANLEIGH." "Ye King's 'Province of Virginia, Novembre 6, 1626 "What was that? Hand it here," snarled the ,A merican Earl. The mild-mannered Marmaduke was roused to revolt. "I jolly well will do nothing of the sort," he retorted. "I bought that deer head at the auction at Stanleigh Hall, Virginia, and carried it over the whole bally United States. It and all in it is mine." Blair moved forward as if to take the paper, but Smythe shoved the library table between himself and the angry Earl, pinning the latter to the wall in a most undignified position. Then the door opened a group of firm-faced men entered. "I beg your pardon, My Lord," said the first of the intruders. "I am Inspector Forde of Scotland Yard. This is an American detective, and he has brought proper requisition papers, and this war- rant has been issued against you." A heavy-set man who towered behind the dapper inspector stepped forward. "I arrest you for the murder of Dr. Henry Lee in Virginia three years ago," he said. Blair moaned and staggered back against the wall. This then was the end—Blake, the Richmond detec- tive, had §truck at last! From the uppermost door of-the overturned taxi- cab a stalwart figure clambered. It was Blair, sometime Earl of Stanleigh! In his hand he held a heavy walking-stick, and, acting with swirt intuition, he turned and thrust the stick through the handle of the door, fastening the door hard and tight. Within the muffled cries of two men zould be heard. De Vaux sprang from his auto and faced Blair in surpriee for one brief moment. And then the fellowship of the desperate, was swiftly invoked.

The traps have got me!" cried Blair. And the two adventurers sprang into the big, undamaged car, which, at a sign from De Vaux, the chaufh t, - backed from the wrecked, overturned taxi, twisted in the broad street. arid darted away. Te; minutes later, from the rooms of De Va,ux, Blair sent the latter, his sworn ally now—such are the strange decrees of destiny—to Vivian with a note, which read:

"Our old friend De Vaux has saved me. 'You hold the fort as Countess of Stanleigh. De Vaux and I will search for The Diamond from the Sky. We are not beaten yet!—Lovingly, Blair." It may be understood that in all the desperate intimacy that. followed De Vaux never let Blair.or Vivian know that he was the mysterious mailed assailant who had struck down Blair in his corona- tion robes and had borne away the great jewel only to drop it in his flight.

In Virginia again there was a gipsy festival, and the little gipsy prince was crowned. At the hill- side fountain that gushed in a crystal stream into the hollow trough that was natUre's own christen- ing font, the minister from Richmond dipped his fingers and sprinkled the son of Esther and Arthur, and said: "I christen thee Arthur Stanleigh Hard- ing!:

A.month after the sensational events in London. while Blair. Vivian, and De Vaux were hiding on the Continent, Marmaduke paid another visit to America. He had studied the strange documents, and then in Virginia searched amongst the ancient colonial records in obscure parishes. Marmaduke had the proofs he required. Those proofs were that Arthur Stanleigh, born son of Hagar and Matt Harding, was strangely enough Arthur Stanleigh in name and right, and, in name and right, the direct descendant in a direct line of the adven- turer, Sir Arthur Stanleigh—and, therefore, right- fully also the heir to the Stanleigh earldom and The Diamond from the Sky. These proofs and the diamond Smythe brought to Esther and Arthur. "We want none of these things for ourselves or for our child," said Arthur, drawing Esther to him tenderly. "Station and wealth bring nothing but sorrow and heartache. The Diamond from the Sky has been a curse and not a charm against harm. It cannot be thrown back to the sky, so let us cast it into the sea and rid the earth of its evil presence. As for the earldom, for myself and my son I deem it better that we be plain American citizens rather than English earls." And Esther earnestly agreed.

"But, your lordship,'" expostulated Smythe, while Arthur smiled at the title, "your lordship may remain an American citizen and still legally hold a British title. I can cite you an instance— several of them." And Smythe did so. The scep- tical may consult Burke's Peerage for the prece- dence in question. "Besides," Smythe went on, "you deal doubly unjustly with her ladyship. Her ladyship Ahould at least be mistress of Stanleigh Hall, as was her mother."

So the world and station called Arthur and Esther Stanleigh back to Stanleigh Hall, and thus the wrongs of many a grievous year were righted.' The guilt of Blair, a fugitive somewhere on the continent, had been known for some months. Arthur, freed from all suspicion of the murder of Dr. Lee, received at Stanleigh Hall, with Esther and their infant son, every heartfelt greeting a generous-minded Virginia welcome could offer. A great reception was ,given them by the high of Fairfax and the humble. Stanleigh Hall, brave in flags, saw happy throngs upon its lawns and within its stately walls again. Vying with the Fairfax band, the gipsy orchestra, led by Quabba, now ruler in Romany, instead of King Arthur and Queen Esther, abdicated in his favour, played again the wild Romany wedding strains. Arthur and Esther, with the ever-attentive Smythe beside them, held the little American earl in their arms. On his baby breast gleamed the great jewel of the Stan- leighs, and ever his flower-faved young motner murmured to herself and to him: "Oh, child of my heart, not, a diamond but a mother's prayer is the true 'charm against harm.' " Love and peace dwell again at Stanleigh Hall. The little American earl, son of Arthur and Esther, has The Diamond from the Sky, and all ends hap- pily, as Hagar prayed, except that somewhere in the world, hidden and perhaps waiting to strike, is the desperate and bitter Blair. With him is his cunning ally, De 'Vauk, and also Vivian, she who is the incarnation of desire for The Diamond from the Sky.

The half-backs as a line were far from good, but individually, Whitfield was the best man on the field. lie worked like a Trojan, and fed his forwards admirably. Several times his work met with enthusiastic applause, especially from the Warringtonians now working at Barrow. Leah was easily the best back on the field, and played with decision. and earnestness. Owen, whose usual position is on the extreme left, was put at full-back, owing to Millward still being on the sick list. div.head: SUMMARY METHOD.
div.p: A SUMMARY METHOD.

The method of breaking in is very summary indeed, and would be regarded on this side as cruel to the horse and not a lit- tle dangerous to the man. There is no pre- liminary parading up and down, and driving round in a circle, and cracking of whipe. The horse to be trained, even though an hour before he knew nothing of man, has to sub- mit at once to be ridden. A halter is first placed on his head, and then a bridle with a ver, strong bit. He protests strongly against ban processes, but the latiga, or short raw hide whip, is brought into play and the animal is made to feel that his pro- tests only bring him punishment. If he is very bad, his I.6gs are lassoed together, and in nearly all cases this has to be done, and the horse thrown, befort the saddle can be put on. The Gaucho's saddle, or recado, is a far more primitive arrangement than what we know by the name, but it is also a great deal more elaborate, having other purposes to serve. A couple of thick cloths, folded, are first placed on the horse's back, and then a pair of pads connected with thongs, one, on each side of the backbone. Over these are placed a very strong, einche, or girth, about seven inches wide, with iron rings at the ends. As the lasso is always attached ,th one of tie rings, the girth has to bear a great strain, and it is pulled so very tight that I think a good deal of cruelty to the horse is involved. On the ton of the einche are placed some rugs and skins, which .at night serve for the Gaucho's bed, and the whole when adjusted makes a very comfort. able sent.

As I have said, in the case of the wild horse, this peculiar saddle is put on whilst the captive animal is panting on the ground, i and learning the lesson that n its relations with man it must always play a subservient part. The Gaucho gets into the saddle, even whilst the horse is on the ground, and then, the feet being rtleasext; the animal- rises and at once the struggle begins. 'He rears and bounds, twists himself almost into a knot in order to rid himself of this strange incubus, but every inovem.snt is met by a lash from the whip and the domina- tion of the horse proceeds. He tries to fall back upon the rider, but a heavy blow be- tween the ears from the loaded handle of tl-e latiga shows, him that this is the worst move of all.

And so the fight gocs on, the horse of course getting the worst of it and becoming gradu- ally exhausted. When this stage has been reached, a second Gaucho mounted on a well- trained animal, appears, riding forward. The wild horse, attraqled by one of his own spe- cies, quickly follows and the second part of the training. ptarts. THE WELL TRAINED ANIMAL.

On the Pampas,, and, indeed all over South America, a sadd:e horse is never\guid- ed, as by us, by pulling at the bit. he pressure of the reins on the neck—much , more admirably I think—is made ,to serve the same turn. The reins being held in the\ left hand, palm upwards, a mere twist guides the horse. A touch on the right of the neck makes the horse go to the left, and vice versa. On the well trained animal a touch of the hand on the neck serves the same pur pose. Indeed, after a time the horses act with the docility and intelligende of trained sheep dogs. I have often rounded up cattlt and corraled other horses without usine either bridle or saddle. But to return to the more direct subject. The rider of the tame animal makes hi: horse twist and wind about, and the wild onr does the same. It is not yet, however, the pressure of the reins but a sharp cut of the latiga on the neck that tells 'him where he must go. When the Gaucho cannot get sufficiently near to the horse he wishes to catch to be able to use the lasso, he takes one of the three balls in his right hand and swings the other two furiously around, like a slinger. When the necessary impetus has been given, he hurls tilt ball forward. The lasso is a long, strong thong of buffalo- hide, with a running noose at one end. It is, thrown in such a way as to fall over the head of the horse, the hunter coiling one end round a high pommel on his saddle. When he makes a successful cast the hunter spurs his horse to the fullest speed and the wild horse is almost strangled or borne to the ground, and becomes an easy prey. Instead of a noose a leaden ball may be attached to the end of the thong, which is thrown so as to entangle the legs or neck of the animal to be captured.

div.head: "All Work and No Play" Woman.
div.p: The "All Work and No Play" Woman.

We all know the woman who starts the day feeling and looking as fresh and as tri.m as a trout fly. It is perfectly ,splendid the way she faces work with. her boots on, as the saying is. But very often she makes a most miserable breakfast and she frequently works in a room poisoned with burnt gas and not a single win- dow open. Before the day is ever ,she has pains in her shoulders and pains in her temper' and all, manner of terrible things on. her tongue. Her back aches; her head aches; her very hair aches. Her legs are tired; her,fiyee are tired; her very skin is tired. She feels stale, leeks stale,' is stale. It's a sorry picture, but it's a true one, and unfortunately, it's a very very common one. If you live in London you may see any number of these "all work and no Play" women going to ,their various offices and shops in the morning; see them rush out for a :bite of lunch at mid-day; go to a pastry Cook's and :gobble up buns and starva- tion sandwiches, tough muffins and jam puffs. Some of them devour cold veal or pork pies; but always these 'deliCacies are washed down with strong tea. Then a bolt is made back to work in the unventilated room orshop. When knock-off time ,comes this busy woman is be- ginning to feel fagged, headaches, and spun out, but more tea whips her up and she pegs away at extra work in the evening. .

Time takes toll. Their eighty-fourth meeting having concluded on Wednesday morning at the Town Hall, the Recruiting Tribunal adjourned for the Christ- mas vacation with a bunch of speeches justifi- ably redolent of satisfaction with the work aecomplished—u something attempted, some- thing don."J It was Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, who created an opening. At the conclusion of the sitting he wished the members of the Tribunal the com- pliments of the season, adding that he knew their duties were of a very --unpleasant and arduous character, and he was sure they would bayle.ased to have a short vacation. He hoped .they would be as happy as the circumstances would allow, and that before another Christmas tame the duties they had to perform would have ceased. _ _ _

On behalf of his colleagues and hfmself, the Chairman Nouncillor Joseph) thanked Mr. Steel for his "kind remarks. "While we have been engaged on this work," he added, "we hake had very few kind regards passed to us, but we have clear consciences, knowing that we have done our best."

Mr. F. A. Frost said he was glad to tell them that he had heard many kind things said about that Tribunal, the opinion having been ex- pressed that the town looked upon it as the best in the country, even by those whom they had had to refuse exemption. The members of the Warrington Tribunal had always attempted to. do their duty impartially, and to him that was a very great satisfaction. He should also like to say that he felt they had had great assistance from the military representatives, who had dis- played fairness in everything, having wanted to do their best for the Army, and, on the other hand, they had done their best for the men individually. • The Chairman: That is a well-deserved tribute to them. Mr. Steel augmented his previous remarks by mentioning that he had had a large experience of various ,Tribunals, and he could honestly state that irtWarrington the Tribunal had never exhibited the least sign of partiality, always showing a desire to get at the facts and judge eases upon their merits. They had held the scales of justice equally. Captain Heaton joined with Mr. Steel in wish- ing the Tribunal members a happy Christmas. He had only been in Warrington. a short time, but he' had been impressed by their fairness and resolve to hold the scales of justice equally between the Army and civilians. • As the members of the Tribunal were leav- ing their seats the Chairman declared faceti- ously, " And now to our next merry meeting!" an expression followed by a colleague (Mr. W. div.p: EVELYN STREET COUNCIL SCHOOL.
Annual Concert.

The girls of the above school crave _their fourth annual concert on Thursday and Friday .of last week, the Central Hall on both occa- sions being filled by an appreciative audience. The "Doll's House l'arty "—a species- of operetta—was full of interest, and partook a good deal of the human element is the wel- come given to the. "guts," whose tit-bits of gossip over their cups of tea reminded one of Mrs. GrUndy. The little mistress playe&the role of hostess with good -grace and .perfect ease. .

The "Triumph,. of Mary June,.",' in "bossing" her mistress, was due—ho sang the nine per- formers-4o the munition factories. The broom and cap were, of course, in evidence, but in Mary Jane's case were symbols' of authority. The humour of this item tickled the audience not a little.

The climax of the evening was the dramatic representation of the favourite Story of "Snow White," with appropriate .action-songs. The pathetic appeal of the princess to the hunts- man, the wicked designs of the Queen, the quaint actions apa. dress of the 'seven dwarfs, and the emotional Wooing of the prince were viv,idly', portrayed by the little _artistes, ,and Consequently received .the weliLmerited . ap- plause of the audience. The same concert--i,the proceeds of which are to. be divided equally between the local War Relief Funds and the- Teachers' Special Fund for supplementing Government allowances, to widows—was repeated on Saturday afternoon for the special ~deleetation Of the wounded soldiers from the various hospitals of the town. The. men sat in wrapt attention throughout the performance, and after,' tea—which was provided by the children themselves—struck up 4 few of .their favourite ditties .to the ac- companiment of one of the teachers on the piano.. Before separating, they cleared the floor for a little dance, when lathe ," Tommy's" efforts at 'lancers caused, no little Merriment to the .onlookers. The outspoken thanks of several, and the happy smiles of more, repaid the efforts of .the.letichers and scholar's it thus providing, a little diversion for the deserving .men.

Grand Matinee To Aid The Memorial Fund.

• Those who wish to participate in the Lord Kitchener. NationakMemorial iFund will have an opportunity of doing so on January 18th, when a grand matinee will take place in the Royal Court Theatre. Already a largenumber Of prominent ladies and gentlemen have prom- ised support. ,With Mr. Harry Warburton .and Mr.- Edmund Osborne as ..organisers, we may be sure that it will be a first-olais programme. The airaof this fund is not to provide a statue —that would merely be an object of admiration. No, the money is to ,be disbursed in doing good to .the men who answered,Kitchener's.call, the fund •being to provide not only medical aid, but to supply appliances, 'expensive nursing requis- ites—such as water beds—and to help to make the life of the disabled soldier as free from dis- comfort as 'possible, to equip and 'endow for all time a home for disabled officers; to establish a permanent fund for the purpose.of relieving dis- abled officers and men in their homes; and to found-a number of,-scholarships, enabling young British soldiers, deStined .• for a comnieroial career: :to travel and gain experience in. The weather of the past week has consi.s-ted of sunshine, fog, rain, severe frost, a heavy fall of snow, and AA attempted thaw_ We live in a very unsettled climate. • And as the "Old Journalist" warned us in the last issue, it has .been ,a universal topic of ceSsversation. Anyhow, I think we have hopes for fairly decent weather this week-end, if not typical 1 Christmas weather. By the way, as Christmas is so near, may I f take this opportunity of wishing you all One of the best." Trusting that by Christmas, 191^, we may all have tasted the sweets of a final victory. .ti I noticed, perhaps with a sense of, regret, that ; quite a good numbsr of skating enthusiasts yen- ; tnred on the (none-too-safe) ice last week-end. ,tC I would like to remind them that' the lake is a very large sheet of watei:, and the ice ought to '1- be strictly tested before it is used for skating. , • So many needless calamities have been caused in the past through people venturing too so-in. What about the fog of last week-end? "Rather thick," I should say. Trains locally were running several hours after their scheduled time, and many passen gers had very unpleasant hours of waiting on the station platform. • . Thanks to our station officials, everything is as done for their comfort, and all the waiting- rooms sported a good fire. Which, under -the circumstances, was very acetptable. I hear that "Monty," one of our favon-ite wounded " Tommies," left the Brookfield Hospi- tal during the past week. He was exceedingly well known throughout the village, and had a vast circle of friends. In fact, he was the olspatient we had, hav- ing been with us the greater part of this year. I hear, through an official of the Post Office, that there are to be no collections in the village on Christmas Eve, other than the ordinary Sun- day collections. So I strongly advise all who desire to send local correspondence for the Christmas Day de- livery to post on Saturday night. I am also informed that most of the Christ- mas pressure will be dealt with by fernale labour. A Post Office trio: Mails, Males and Fe-males. I am pleased to say that quite a good number .of local soldiers have arrived home for Christ maa. The remainder, no doubt, will arrive for Cie 'New Year. What a lot of licensing cases we have had just lately, compared' with what we used to -have. What is the reason? Are the po,lice get'iag very vigilant! Or are the licensees forgetting themselves? The Act certainly gives them little scope.

106 Appointments,;. 530 Certificates. :The. year. 1916 at .Wood's College has.been a very successful one—for public commercial ex- amination successes and for appointments. The annual presentation of prizes and Certificates took place on Wednesday, when the College broke up for the. Christmas vacation. The awards were presented by .Mrs. F. Wilson Wood. The chair was occupied by the Prin- cipal, and his report was highly satisfactory. In the course of a short address, the Prin- cipal conveyed some very useful practical hints with regard to commercial training, urging the students to gain proficiency in shorthand and typewriting, because there was pp doubt that those who were thoroughly qualified got the best salaries. Wood's College was a pre-war institution, and since its inception—now several years back—it had developed into a large and influential establishment, and the present spacious new building had been neces- sary to accommodate day students flocking to the clas.ses: The staff of the college laboured ceaselessly in the endeavour • to aid the students, and he was glad to say that the in4titution was patronised by pupils of more than average ability. As a result of the efforts of Wood's College,' he was able to trace at least. 106 direct appointments during the past year through the College Employment Bureau; while. over 530 certificates had been gained during that time—such results spoke for them- selves. -Every pupil qualified to take up a posi- tion had been provided with a satisfactory appointment; and if there were even three times the number of pupils in daily attend- ance. he could undertake to 'find places for them all as soon as their training under his personal superrigion was finished. The Principal 'announced that for the, new term, Which commences January 3rd, a mutt- her of improvements were being made, which would benefit the students. Votes of thanks and presentations from the pupils, together with a collection in aid of ,local Red Cross Funds, concluded the pro- ceedings. The lists of awards have appeared from time to time in "The Examiner."

Shaken in health by his wife's death a few months ago, Mr. Fairhurst went to Southport .in the ,hope that the change would do him good. On Saturday, however, he met with a chill, which developed to bronchial' pneumonia, and he died as stated.
